title: Newton's Identities: Power Sums and Elementary Symmetric Polynomials
description: Newton's identities express power sums pₖ = Σxᵢᵏ in terms of elementary symmetric polynomials eⱼ. Proved for 2, 3, and 4 variables: the recursive form pₖ = Σ(-1)^{i-1} eᵢ pₖ₋ᵢ + (-1)^{k-1} k eₖ, plus the inversion formulas recovering eₖ from power sums. Applications to discriminants, matrix traces, and the sum-of-cubes factorization.

meta.author: Isaac Newton (1707); formalized here

mathlibDependencies.description: Ring tactic for polynomial identity verification

originalContributions: Newton's identities for 2 variables: p₁ through p₆ via recurrence pₖ = e₁·pₖ₋₁ − e₂·pₖ₋₂
Newton's identities for 3 variables: p₁ through p₅ via recurrence pₖ = e₁·pₖ₋₁ − e₂·pₖ₋₂ + e₃·pₖ₋₃
Newton's identities for 4 variables: p₂, p₃, p₄ via the full 4-variable recurrence
Pure expressions: pₖ in terms of elementary symmetric polynomials only (eliminating intermediate power sums)
Inversion formulas: recover e₂ and e₃ from power sums p₁, p₂, p₃ over a field
Discriminant formulas: quadratic and cubic discriminants via elementary symmetric polynomials
Matrix trace connection: characteristic polynomial coefficients from traces via Newton's identities
Sum-of-cubes factorization: x³ + y³ + z³ − 3xyz = (x+y+z)(x²+y²+z² − xy − xz − yz)
meta.notes: Newton's identities are fundamental to symmetric function theory. They bridge Vieta's formulas (coefficients ↔ roots) with power sum invariants, and underpin the Cayley-Hamilton theorem, characteristic polynomial computation, and Galois theory.

sections.title: Two Variables
sections.description: Newton's identities for elementary symmetric polynomials e₁ = x+y, e₂ = xy and power sums pₖ = xᵏ+yᵏ. The recurrence pₖ = e₁·pₖ₋₁ − e₂·pₖ₋₂ proved for k = 1 through 6.

sections.title: Three Variables
sections.description: Newton's identities for e₁, e₂, e₃ and power sums in three variables. Both recursive form (pₖ via previous power sums) and pure form (pₖ via elementary symmetric polynomials only).

sections.title: Four Variables
sections.description: Newton's identities for four variables, including the full fourth identity p₄ = e₁·p₃ − e₂·p₂ + e₃·p₁ − 4·e₄.

sections.title: Inversion
sections.description: Recovering elementary symmetric polynomials from power sums: e₂ = (p₁² − p₂)/2 and e₃ = (p₁³ − 3p₁p₂ + 2p₃)/6.

sections.title: Applications
sections.description: Discriminant formulas (quadratic and cubic), matrix trace identities, Cayley-Hamilton in trace form, and the sum-of-cubes factorization.

overview.what: Newton's identities express power sums pₖ = Σxᵢᵏ as explicit polynomials in the elementary symmetric polynomials eⱼ, and vice versa.
overview.whyMatters: These identities are foundational to symmetric function theory and connect polynomial coefficients (Vieta's formulas) to trace-like invariants. They underpin the Cayley-Hamilton theorem, spectral theory, and are essential in Galois theory.
overview.approach: Direct algebraic verification using the ring tactic for 2, 3, and 4 variables. Each Newton identity is a polynomial identity that ring closes automatically. Inversion uses field_simp + ring.
overview.keyInsight: The recurrence pₖ = Σᵢ₌₁ⁿ (−1)^{i−1} eᵢ · pₖ₋ᵢ is a universal identity that holds for any number of variables n. For k > n, the eₖ term vanishes and the recurrence simplifies.

conclusion.summary: All 31 theorems proved with 0 sorries and 0 axioms. Newton's identities verified for 2, 3, and 4 variables in both recursive and pure forms, with applications to discriminants and matrix traces.
